title: Your verses
hookLine: the ten Dhammapada verses you chose in year one, and what they mean now
tomorrow: who took refuge when there were only two jewels?

cards: A song you played on repeat at twelve can sound like a different song at seventeen. Same words. Different listener.
Some lines from childhood still fit; some read like they were written for someone else. In year one you chose ten verses from the Dhammapada and kept them. They haven't changed a letter since.
So here's today's question: what does a verse do in a life, if you keep it long enough? Mai found one answer in two kitchens, a few miles apart.

teach.b: The Dhammapada is short on purpose: verses made to be carried, memorized, said under the breath.

teach.h: ALL THAT WE ARE: WHAT WE HAVE THOUGHT.
teach.b: Its first lines, in Max Müller's old translation: all that we are is the result of what we have thought.

The verse goes on: act from a harmful mind, and pain follows, like the wheel behind the ox; act from a pure mind, and happiness follows, like a shadow that never leaves. Ông keeps a card with that verse on his fridge.
Mai's friend Ava has a grandmother who keeps a line from the Bible framed by her stove, from the book of Proverbs: keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
Here's what the two share, and it's real. Both say the life that comes out of you starts inside you. Watch the inside, and the outside follows.
Proverbs is a book that says the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; the heart is kept before God. The Dhammapada traces the mind and its fruits, and names no creator at all.
Neither one needs to become the other. And the answer to today's question: a verse you keep long enough starts reading you.
The verses stayed. The reader didn't.

how: Many Buddhists memorize and recite Dhammapada verses, and some keep a favorite written where they'll see it; in Theravada communities the verses are chanted and often taught to children.

games.q: your friend's family has a Bible verse on the wall, and yours has a Buddhist one. your friend asks, 'so are our religions the same?' what's the honest reply?
o: some things are truly shared, like watching your heart; some are truly different, like God's place in it.
yes, all religions are the same underneath; the words just differ.
no, nothing in them overlaps; they don't share a single idea.
games.why: both verses say the life comes from inside. Proverbs keeps that heart before God; the Dhammapada names no creator. shared, and honestly different.

practice: Open your list of ten, or recall the ones you can. Read each once, slowly. Pick the one that reads differently now than it did in year one, and copy it by hand, letter by letter, as slowly as the sit allows.

wordCard.voice: Your verses: the ten from the Dhammapada you chose in year one. Same words. A different reader, five years on.
